analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage in steps to $25 an hour and ends subminimum wages for tipped, young, and disabled workers.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2026 with four Democratic cosponsors and referred to the Senate labor committee, where it has sat with no hearings, no markup, and no vote; the session ends in January 2027.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise the federal minimum wage from $7.25 an hour in scheduled steps to $25 an hour, with the largest, most profitable corporations required to get there fastest. Big companies would reach $25 within five years and the minimum would then rise automatically with the national median wage; smaller employers would have twelve years to catch up. It would also phase out the separate lower wages that currently let employers pay tipped workers, newly hired teenagers, and some workers with disabilities below the minimum, ending those subminimum wages entirely once the transition wages converge with the standard minimum.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers currently paid at or near the $7.25 federal minimum, especially tipped restaurant workers, workers with disabilities now paid under special certificates, and teen hires, all of whom would see large, scheduled raises. The bill's findings state the goal is to reduce reliance on public assistance by making work pay a living wage.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum from $7.25 to $12 an hour on the effective date, then in annual steps to $25 for large employers within five years.
Gives smaller employers a slower schedule reaching $25 after twelve years, so the largest and most profitable corporations lead the transition.

Raises the tipped-worker cash wage for large employers from $6 to the full minimum within five years, and phases out the separate tipped minimum entirely for all employers once the small-employer cash wage reaches the standard minimum.

Repeals the subminimum wage for newly hired workers under 20 and phases out special certificates allowing subminimum pay for workers with disabilities, while directing the Labor Department to help those workers transition to competitive integrated employment.
After the transition, indexes the minimum to two-thirds of the national median hourly wage so it rises with the economy instead of waiting on Congress.

analysis.who_pays: Large employers with $1 billion or more in annual revenue or 500 or more employees pay the steepest increases first; restaurant and hospitality employers lose the tipped subminimum, and holders of disability subminimum certificates eventually lose the authority altogether. Consumers may bear some of this through higher prices, especially in food service.

drawbacks.text: Mandated raises of this size, roughly tripling the federal minimum within five years for big employers, could raise prices at restaurants and other low-wage sectors, accelerate automation, and squeeze employers in lower-wage regions where $25 an hour exceeds prevailing wages.

The bill creates a two-tier wage floor for over a decade: a worker at a small employer could legally be paid $20.60 in year five while the same job at a large employer must pay $25, and small employers only reach $25 after twelve years.

The phase-out of subminimum certificates for workers with disabilities could reduce paid workshop opportunities for some workers if competitive integrated jobs are not available in their area, which is why the bill directs the Labor Department to provide transition assistance.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the millions of workers paid near the federal minimum, the raises are large and scheduled, which is the core benefit. The costs are real but spread: higher prices in low-wage service industries, a longer adjustment runway for small employers, and genuine transition risk for some workers with disabilities. The main honest objection is pace and geography, not the goal.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on July 14, 2026, read twice, and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which has taken no action on it; the session ends January 3, 2027.

narrative.text: Sen. Chris Murphy introduced the Living Wage For All Act in the Senate on July 14, 2026, joined by Sens. Blumenthal, Wyden, and Kim.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day, with no further action listed in the record.
It has four cosponsors, all Democrats, and no Republican support is recorded.

The bill text sets the wage floor at $12 an hour immediately, $25 for large employers within five years, $25 for other employers within twelve years, and phases out the tipped, youth, and disability subminimum wages.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, employers that pay at or near the $7.25 federal minimum, including restaurant chains and large low-wage employers, are better off than they would be under the bill, since no wage increases have been scheduled or debated. Workers gain nothing yet.

for.name: Sen. Chris Murphy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and set the structure: large employers reach $25 an hour fastest, then the minimum indexes to the national median wage.

for.name: Sens. Richard Blumenthal, Ron Wyden, and Andy Kim

sides.party_line_note: No vote has been held and no committee action recorded, so no opposition positions are on the record; the four sponsors and cosponsors are all Democrats, suggesting a partisan split if it ever advanced.

industries.note: They face the steepest schedule, from $12 to $25 an hour within five years. Their payroll cost is the wage gain for millions of workers, though some of it may come back as higher prices.

The bill raises the tipped cash wage for large employers to the full minimum within five years and ends the separate tipped minimum altogether, moving wage income from employer payroll savings to servers and bussers.

New certificates are banned immediately and existing ones expire once transition wages reach the standard minimum; the bill directs the Labor Department to help affected workers move to competitive jobs.

They still must raise wages to $25 but get twelve years instead of five, easing the cost while creating a two-tier floor in which the same work can legally pay less at a small business for over a decade.

analysis.trajectory: The realistic path is that it dies in committee. It was referred in mid-July of an election-session year with the session ending January 3, 2027, has no committee action scheduled or recorded, and has no Republican cosponsors, which at this stage means no committee markup and no floor vote.
